label: Autocovariance of AR processes — mastery test (unseen)

items.stem: The variance of a stationary AR(1) process with coefficient φ and shock variance σ² is:
items.explanation: From γ₀ = φγ₁ + σ² and γ₁ = φγ₀, substituting gives γ₀ = φ²γ₀ + σ², hence γ₀ = σ²/(1 − φ²). The σ² term comes from E(yₜεₜ), which is not zero because yₜ contains εₜ.
items.check: The variance is at least σ² because the current innovation contributes σ² and all additional squared weights are non-negative; it is strictly greater when φ ≠ 0.

items.stem: The autocorrelation at lag k of an AR(1) process is:
items.explanation: Multiplying the model by yₜ₋ₖ and taking expectations gives γₖ = φγₖ₋₁, so γₖ = φᵏγ₀ and ρₖ = φᵏ. Simulated at φ = 0.7: 0.7001, 0.4903, 0.3433 at lags 1, 2, 3.
items.check: At k = 0 this gives ρ₀ = 1, as any autocorrelation function must.

items.stem: In deriving the autocovariances of an AR process, the term σ² appears in:
items.explanation: E(yₜ₋ₖεₜ) = 0 for k ≥ 1, because yₜ₋ₖ is built from shocks dated t−k and earlier. Only at k = 0 does the cross term survive, as E(yₜεₜ) = σ². That is why the recursion for k ≥ 1 is homogeneous and the variance needs a separate equation.

items.stem: For an AR(1) with φ = 0.5 and σ² = 1, the variance is:
items.explanation: γ₀ = 1/(1 − 0.25) = 1/0.75 = 1.3333. This equals Σφ^(2j) = 1 + 0.25 + 0.0625 + ⋯, the sum from the MA(∞) representation.
items.check: It must exceed 1 = σ², which it does.

items.stem: The autocorrelations of an AR process depend on:
items.explanation: ρₖ = φᵏ for an AR(1) and the recursion for higher orders — in each case a function of the coefficients alone. Multiplying σ² by a constant scales every γₖ equally, leaving the ratios unchanged. The shock variance sets the scale, the coefficients set the shape.

items.stem: The autocovariances of an AR(2) satisfy, for k ≥ 1:
items.explanation: Multiplying the model by yₜ₋ₖ for k ≥ 1 and taking expectations gives exactly this, with the σ² term absent because E(yₜ₋ₖεₜ) = 0. The same relation holds in ρ after dividing by γ₀.

items.stem: For an AR(2) process, the lag-1 autocorrelation is:
items.explanation: The k = 1 equation reads ρ₁ = φ₁ + φ₂ρ₋₁, and ρ₋₁ = ρ₁ by symmetry, so ρ₁(1 − φ₂) = φ₁. The symmetry is essential: without it the equation cannot be solved. At (0.5, 0.3) the value is 0.5/0.7 = 0.7143, simulated 0.7145.
items.check: Setting φ₂ = 0 must recover ρ₁ = φ₁, the AR(1) case, which it does.

items.stem: For an AR(2) with φ = (0.5, 0.3) and σ² = 1, the variance is:
items.explanation: γ₀ = σ²(1−φ₂)/[(1+φ₂)((1−φ₂)²−φ₁²)] = 0.7/(1.3 × (0.49 − 0.25)) = 0.7/0.312 = 2.2436, simulated 2.2466. It exceeds the 1.3333 an AR(1) with φ = 0.5 would give, because the second lag adds persistence.
items.check: The step-by-step route gives the same: γ₀(1 − 0.5ρ₁ − 0.3ρ₂) = 1 with ρ₁ = 0.7143 and ρ₂ = 0.6571 yields 1/0.4457 = 2.2436.

items.stem: An AR(2) with φ = (0.5, 0.3) has lag-2 autocorrelation:
items.explanation: ρ₂ = φ₁ρ₁ + φ₂ρ₀ = 0.5(0.7143) + 0.3(1) = 0.3571 + 0.3 = 0.6571, simulated 0.6577. Note it is larger than ρ₁² = 0.5102 would be, so the decay is slower than geometric.
items.check: The recursion then gives ρ₃ = 0.5(0.6571) + 0.3(0.7143) = 0.5429, simulated 0.5432.

items.stem: The variance of an AR(1) at φ = −0.7 compared with φ = +0.7 is:
options: identical, since γ₀ depends on φ²
items.explanation: γ₀ = σ²/(1 − φ²) sees only φ², so both give 1.9608 at σ² = 1. The ACFs differ — φᵏ alternates when φ is negative — so the sign changes the shape without changing the magnitude. Keeping those two readings separate avoids a common confusion.

items.stem: Consider the autocovariance structure of AR processes.
items.explanation: A is true and is the commonest error to avoid. B is true: the recursion is homogeneous, so only the k = 0 equation fixes the scale. C is true — the variance is at least σ² for a stationary AR process because the MA(∞) representation has ψ₀ = 1 and the remaining squared weights are non-negative; equality occurs for white noise and the inequality is strict otherwise. D is false: the symmetry γ₋ₖ = γₖ is essential, since the AR(2) k = 1 equation cannot be solved without recognising γ₋₁ as γ₁.
statements: For an AR(2), ρ₁ is φ₁/(1 − φ₂) rather than φ₁.
The recursion for k ≥ 1 determines the shape of the autocovariance function but not its scale.
The variance of a stationary AR process is at least σ².
The symmetry γ₋ₖ = γₖ plays no role in the AR(2) derivation.

A.why: True. The k = 1 equation involves γ₋₁, which must be identified with γ₁, and solving gives ρ₁(1 − φ₂) = φ₁. At (0.5, 0.3) that is 0.7143, not 0.5.

B.why: True — the recursion is homogeneous, so multiplying every γ by a constant preserves it. The scale comes from the k = 0 equation, the only one with a σ² term.

C.why: True. The current innovation contributes σ² and all past-shock weights add non-negative squared terms, so γ₀ = σ²Σψⱼ² ≥ σ². Equality occurs for white noise (all AR coefficients zero); otherwise the inequality is strict.

D.why: False — it is essential. Without γ₋₁ = γ₁ the k = 1 equation has an unknown on the wrong side and the derivation of ρ₁ = φ₁/(1 − φ₂) does not go through.

items.stem: An AR(1) has variance 2.7778 with σ² = 1. The modulus of its coefficient is:
items.explanation: Inverting γ₀ = 1/(1 − φ²): 1 − φ² = 1/2.7778 = 0.36, so φ² = 0.64 and |φ| = 0.8. The sign is not determined by the variance — ρ₁ would settle it.

items.stem: An AR(2) with φ = (0.6, 0.5) is substituted into the variance formula, which returns a negative value. The correct reading is:
options: the formula applies only to AR(1) processes
an arithmetic error has been made
the shock variance must be negative
the coefficients are outside the stationarity region, so no autocovariance function exists
items.explanation: φ₁ + φ₂ = 1.1 > 1 violates the first stationarity condition, so no stationary autocovariance function exists. The displayed variance formula was derived under stationarity; for this particular pair it returns a negative algebraic value, signalling the failed precondition. But positivity of the formal expression is not a general stationarity test, because outside the stationary region both numerator and denominator can be negative.

items.stem: An AR(2) with φ = (0.5, −0.2) has lag-2 autocorrelation approximately:
items.explanation: ρ₁ = 0.5/(1 − (−0.2)) = 0.5/1.2 = 0.4167, then ρ₂ = 0.5(0.4167) + (−0.2)(1) = 0.2083 − 0.2 = 0.0083. The negative second coefficient both enlarges the denominator for ρ₁ and subtracts in the recursion, so the ACF collapses almost to zero by lag 2.
items.check: The two lags are working against each other here, unlike the (0.5, 0.3) case where ρ₂ stayed high at 0.6571.

items.stem: An AR(2) process has an autocorrelation function that oscillates and crosses zero repeatedly. This indicates:
items.explanation: When φ₁² + 4φ₂ < 0 the characteristic equation z² − φ₁z − φ₂ = 0 has a complex conjugate pair, so the difference equation's solution is a damped sine ρₖ = Crᵏ sin(ωk + δ) with r = √|φ₂|. It is still a pure AR(2), with a PACF cutting off at lag 2.

items.stem: For an AR(1) with φ = 0.95 and σ² = 1, the variance is approximately:
items.explanation: 1/(1 − 0.9025) = 1/0.0975 = 10.2564. The amplification factor grows sharply near the unit circle: 1.33 at φ = 0.5, 2.78 at 0.8, 5.26 at 0.9 and 10.26 at 0.95, diverging as φ approaches 1.
items.check: A persistent process must be far more variable than its shocks, which rules out the small options at once.

items.stem: Consider the AR(2) variance formula and its structure.
items.explanation: A is true — the difference of squares factors that way, and the three factors are the three stationarity conditions. B is true: setting φ₂ = 0 must give the AR(1) result, and it does. C is true, and it is correct because yₜ = φ₂yₜ₋₂ + εₜ is two interleaved AR(1) processes. D is false — the formula gives γ₀, and higher autocovariances come from the recursion.
statements: At φ₂ = 0 the formula reduces to σ²/(1 − φ₁²).
At φ₁ = 0 it reduces to σ²/(1 − φ₂²).
The formula gives γₖ for every lag k directly.

A.why: True: (1−φ₂)² − φ₁² is a difference of squares. Positivity of all three denominator factors is equivalent to the stationarity triangle. Under stationarity the numerator 1−φ₂ is also positive, giving a positive variance. However, outside stationarity the numerator and denominator can both be negative, so a positive algebraic value does not prove stationarity; the formula is derived under the stationary-model assumption.

B.why: True, and it is a necessary check on any AR(2) derivation: with φ₂ = 0 the process IS an AR(1), so the formula must collapse to σ²/(1 − φ₁²).

C.why: True, and correct for a reason worth seeing: yₜ = φ₂yₜ₋₂ + εₜ links only times of the same parity, so the odd- and even-indexed observations each form an AR(1) in φ₂ with the same variance σ²/(1 − φ₂²).

D.why: False. It gives γ₀ alone. The higher autocovariances follow from γₖ = φ₁γₖ₋₁ + φ₂γₖ₋₂ once γ₀ and γ₁ are known.

items.stem: For an AR(2) with φ = (1.2, −0.4) and σ² = 1, the lag-1 autocorrelation is:
items.explanation: ρ₁ = φ₁/(1 − φ₂) = 1.2/(1 − (−0.4)) = 1.2/1.4 = 0.8571. Note the negative φ₂ enlarges the denominator to 1.4, so ρ₁ falls below φ₁ even though φ₁ exceeds 1 — and the process is stationary, since 0.8 < 1, −1.6 < 1 and 0.4 < 1 all hold.
items.check: ρ₁ must lie in [−1, 1], which rules out the value 1.2 immediately.

items.stem: Why does the difference equation γₖ = φ₁γₖ₋₁ + φ₂γₖ₋₂ not by itself determine the autocovariance function?
options: it holds only for k = 1 and k = 2
it is homogeneous, so it fixes the shape but not the scale, which the k = 0 equation supplies
it requires complex roots to be solvable
it determines the scale but not the shape
items.explanation: Multiplying every γₖ by any constant still satisfies the recursion, so it cannot pin down the magnitude. The scale is set by the k = 0 equation γ₀ = φ₁γ₁ + φ₂γ₂ + σ², the only one containing σ². That is the structural reason the variance is computed separately rather than falling out of the recursion.

items.stem: Sample variance estimates from an AR(1) with φ = 0.95 and n = 200 scatter widely and tend to fall below the theoretical 10.26. The main reasons are:
options: the shocks not being normally distributed
an error in the theoretical formula
a small effective sample size, and downward bias from centring on the sample mean
items.explanation: The effective sample size is roughly n(1−φ)/(1+φ) ≈ 5 at these values, so even an unbiased estimator would scatter badly. On top of that, the sample variance is computed around the sample mean, which for a persistent series tracks wherever the realisation happened to wander — so subtracting it removes genuine variation and biases the estimate downward. Both effects shrink as φ moves away from 1.
